lessons.title: Constructing a concrete base for a tank
lessons.html:
Why the base matters

Water is heavy: one cubic metre weighs about one tonne. A 10 000 litre tank full of water puts about 10 tonnes on its base. If the base is uneven or settles, the tank can crack, bulge, lean or collapse, which is a serious safety hazard and a costly loss. Most tank manufacturers will not honour warranties unless the base meets their specification.

Choosing the site

  • Firm, undisturbed ground; avoid filled ground, termite mounds, clay that swells, or areas that flood.
  • Away from tree roots that can lift the slab and from overhead power lines.
  • Access for delivery trucks and for maintenance.
  • Height: placing the tank higher gives more gravity pressure (about 1 bar per 10 m height), but stands must be designed by a competent person.
  • Check local by-laws and estate rules.

Building the slab

  1. Mark out the slab larger than the tank diameter, as the manufacturer requires.
  2. Excavate topsoil and organic matter down to firm ground.
  3. Compact the base in layers with a plate compactor, using suitable fill such as G5 gravel if needed.
  4. Set up formwork (shutters) level, using a spirit level, line level or dumpy level.
  5. Place a damp-proof membrane if specified, and steel reinforcing mesh on spacers so it sits within the concrete, not on the ground.
  6. Leave sleeves or conduits for outlet pipes, drains or cables if they pass through the slab.
  7. Pour concrete of the strength specified, compact it with a poker or by rodding, and level with a screed board. The top must be flat and smooth, with no stones sticking out that could damage a plastic tank base.
  8. Cure the concrete by keeping it damp and covered for several days before loading.

Safety

Wet cement burns skin: wear gloves, boots, long sleeves and eye protection. Lift bags correctly. Keep excavations barricaded.

lessons.title: Positioning the tank and installing piping
lessons.html:
Positioning the tank

  1. Check the slab is cured, level and clean. Sweep off stones and grit.
  2. Inspect the tank for transport damage before unloading.
  3. Lift and move the tank with enough people or with slings and a crane truck as appropriate. Never roll a tank over rough ground, and never lift it by its fittings.
  4. Place the tank centrally so the whole base is supported, with outlets facing the direction of the pipes.
  5. Secure against wind when empty: an empty plastic tank is light and can blow over. Use tie-downs or straps where the manufacturer recommends.

Pipe connections

ConnectionPurpose and installation points
InletUsually at the top; supply from municipal line, borehole or gutters, with a float valve or switch controlling the level
OutletNear the bottom, slightly above the floor so sediment is not drawn into the pump; fit a strainer
OverflowNear the top, same size or larger than the inlet; leads water safely away from the slab and buildings, with an insect screen
Drain or scourAt the lowest point, with a valve, for cleaning
VentLets air in and out as water level changes; screened

Installing pipes

  • Use tank connectors (bulkhead fittings) with the correct seals; tighten as the manufacturer says without cracking the tank wall.
  • Use flexible connectors between the tank and rigid pipes, because tanks move slightly as they fill.
  • Support pipes so their weight does not hang on the tank fittings.
  • Where a tank is filled from a municipal supply, the inlet must have an air gap above the overflow level or a backflow device, so tank water cannot flow back into the drinking water main, as municipal by-laws require.
  • Protect plastic pipes above ground from sunlight with UV-resistant pipe or covering.

Safety

Never enter a tank: it is a confined space, and entry needs a permit, gas testing and a standby person under OHS confined space rules. Do work from outside.

lessons.title: Fitting valves and float switches
lessons.html:
Isolation and control valves

  • Isolating valve on the outlet: a gate or ball valve next to the tank so pipes and pumps can be serviced without draining the tank.
  • Isolating valve on the inlet: to stop filling during maintenance.
  • Non-return valve: on pump suction or delivery where water must not flow back.
  • Scour valve: on the drain outlet.
  • Float valve (ball valve): a mechanical valve on the inlet that closes as a float rises, keeping the tank from overflowing.

Fit valves with unions so they can be removed. Check flow arrows. Test that each valve opens and closes fully.

Adjusting a mechanical float valve

  1. Fill the tank and watch the level at which the float valve closes.
  2. Adjust the float arm or float position so the valve closes a safe distance below the overflow.
  3. Check the valve closes fully with no dripping; replace washers if needed.

Float switches

Float switches are electrical switches that tilt or move with the water level. They control pumps:

UseAction
Filling a tank from a boreholeStop the borehole pump when the tank is full; start it when the level drops
Pumping out of a tank to irrigationStop the irrigation pump when the tank is nearly empty (dry-run protection)
AlarmWarn of high or low level

Fitting and adjusting float switches

  • Clamp the cable to a fixed point, inside the tank or on a weighted bracket, so the float tilts freely without touching the wall, pipes or other floats.
  • The tether length sets the difference between on and off levels: longer tether, bigger range.
  • Set the low-level switch so the pump stops while the outlet is still under water.
  • Wiring to the pump panel must be done by a qualified electrician.
  • Test by raising and lowering the float and confirming the pump starts and stops.

Records

Record tank size, slab details, valve and float settings, and test results, and give the client a simple drawing of the connections.

Key points

  • A full tank is very heavy; build a level, reinforced, cured concrete base.
  • Place outlets above the floor, fit overflow, drain and vent with screens.
  • Use flexible connectors and support pipes; protect municipal supplies from backflow.
  • Fit isolating valves and adjust float valves below overflow level.
  • Use float switches for pump control and dry-run protection; never enter a tank.
